summary.text: Total internal reflection is when a wave reaching a boundary is sent completely back into the first medium instead of passing into the second.
It needs the second medium to have a lower refractive index and the wave to arrive at an angle beyond a threshold called the critical angle.
It keeps light inside optical fibers and binocular prisms, and it makes the water surface look like a mirror when seen from below.

facts.label: Water to air
facts.value: Critical angle of about 49 degrees for visible light

facts.label: Glass to air
facts.value: Critical angle of about 42 degrees for common glass

facts.label: Direction rule
facts.value: Possible from higher to lower refractive index, never the reverse

facts.label: Fresnel, 1823
facts.value: His explanation of its phase shifts supported the wave theory of light

facts.label: Evanescent wave
facts.value: A fading wave travels along the boundary in the outer medium

items.prompt: You stand beside an aquarium with your eyes below the water level and see fish reflected in the water surface as clearly as the real ones. What is happening?

options.label: The surface absorbs light and re-emits a copy of the fish
The glass tank magnifies and flips the fish image
Water scatters light so that it bounces in all directions
Light hitting the surface at a steep slant is entirely reflected back down

items.explain: Past the critical angle there is no refracted ray, so the reflection becomes total, as bright as the direct view.

items.prompt: Could light inside the air above a pool be totally reflected at the water surface, if it hits at a very slanted angle?

options.label: No, because it is going from a lower to a higher refractive index
Yes, any very slanted ray will always do it
Yes, but only if the water is perfectly still
No, because water never reflects light

items.explain: Total internal reflection cannot occur for rare-to-dense incidence, such as air to water; it is possible only from the denser medium into the rarer one.

items.prompt: Phone calls and internet data travel as light through a thin glass strand for miles without leaking out of its sides. What keeps the light inside?

options.label: Total internal reflection at the strand's walls
A thick metal coating that absorbs stray light
Light being slowed until it can barely move
The glass magnifying the beam to fill the strand

items.explain: Optical fibers exploit the efficiency of total internal reflection to carry light along their length.

items.prompt: A diver aims a torch up at the surface and tilts it to a more and more slanted angle. What happens to the beam that leaves the water?

options.label: It grows steadily brighter outside the water
It bends toward the surface, skims along it, then vanishes
It bends toward the vertical and exits straight up
It splits into several beams of different colors

items.explain: As the angle approaches the critical angle, the refracted ray approaches 90 degrees and runs along the boundary; beyond it there is no refracted ray.

items.prompt: In the ideal case, total internal reflection returns every bit of the light. What can make it noticeably less than total?

options.label: Making the ray meet the boundary more steeply
Using a much larger piece of glass for it
Putting an absorbing object close to the boundary
Waiting until the light has faded in color

items.explain: If the evanescent wave in the outer medium is absorbed or diverted by objects there, the reflection falls short of total.

items.prompt: Glass has a higher refractive index than water. Going by the critical angles for glass-to-air and water-to-air, which boundary traps light with a smaller tilt from the perpendicular?

options.label: Water to air, because water is clearer than glass
Water to air, because it is the denser material
Water to air, because its critical angle is lower
Glass to air, because its critical angle is lower

items.explain: The critical angle is about 42 degrees for glass to air and about 49 degrees for water to air, so glass starts trapping light at a smaller angle.

paragraphs.heading: Trapped at the boundary
paragraphs.text: Total internal reflection, or TIR, happens when a wave reaches the boundary between two materials and none of it crosses over. Instead, all of it bounces back into the first material. Two things are needed: the second material must have a lower refractive index, meaning waves move faster in it, and the wave must strike the boundary at a wide enough slant.

paragraphs.heading: The critical angle
paragraphs.text: When light passes from water into air, the angle between the outgoing ray and the surface normal is larger than that of the incoming ray. As the incoming angle grows, the outgoing ray tilts further until, at a threshold called the critical angle, it reaches 90° and skims along the surface. Past that angle there is no way for the light to refract, so no ray goes out and all of it is reflected. For visible light the critical angle is about 49° from water into air and about 42° from common glass into air.

paragraphs.heading: Only from dense to rare
paragraphs.text: The material with the higher refractive index is called optically denser, and the other one optically rarer. Total internal reflection can only happen going from dense to rare, never from rare to dense. So light going from air into water cannot be totally reflected. In symbols, θ_c = arcsin (n₂/n₁), and this has a value only when n₂ ≤ n₁.

paragraphs.heading: The mirror in the aquarium
paragraphs.text: Stand next to an aquarium with your eyes below the water line, and you will often see fish and objects reflected in the surface above. The reflection looks just as bright as the direct view, which can be startling. You can see the same thing by opening your eyes while swimming just under calm water. Past the critical angle, the surface looks like a mirror reflecting what is below.

paragraphs.heading: Not quite total
paragraphs.text: No energy keeps flowing across the boundary, yet the outer material still carries a so-called evanescent wave. It runs along the boundary and fades quickly with distance from it. If the outer material absorbs that wave, or something nearby picks it up, the reflection becomes noticeably less than total.

paragraphs.heading: Putting it to work
paragraphs.text: Because the reflection is so efficient, optical fibers use it to guide light in telecommunications cables and in fiberscopes that form images. Reflecting prisms in binoculars and monoculars use it too. In 1823 Augustin-Jean Fresnel explained the shifts this reflection causes in the light wave, which strengthened the case that light is a wave. His invention, the Fresnel rhomb, uses those shifts to change light's polarization.

paragraphs.heading: Not just light
paragraphs.text: The effect is most familiar with light, but it happens with other waves as well. Microwaves, sound waves and water waves can all be totally reflected. A simple demonstration sends a narrow beam of light into a half-cylinder of glass or acrylic.
